st.an: The source’s recoverable passages concern conformity in advocacy, possible lawyer displacement, an illustrative ChatGPT exchange, and virtual proceedings. It does not, however, supply measured performance evidence or directly address verification standards.

st.an: The dossier accepts the cluster’s core view that AI use remains subject to human accountability and verification, while materially extending it through a concrete rulemaking debate. st.t: AI privilege: Legal subject matter is insufficient
st.an: The commenter supports the cluster’s qualified conclusion that AI-related legal workflows are not automatically protected, expressly conceding that chosen research tools probably lack work-product protection. kp.k: Proposed certification linked AI drafting to human verification
kp.d: The November 2023 proposal would require counsel and unrepresented filers to certify either non-use of generative AI in drafting or human review and approval of all generated text, including citations and legal analysis. It permitted AI-assisted drafting rather than banning it. A material misrepresentation could result in striking the filing and sanctions against the signatory.
qs: Additionally, counsel and unrepresented filers must further certify that no generative artificial intelligence program was used in drafting the document presented for filing, or to the extent such a program was used, all generated text, including all citations and legal analysis, has been reviewed for accuracy and approved by a human.
A material misrepresentation in the certificate of compliance may result in striking the document and sanctions against the person signing the document.

kp.k: Court declined certification while preserving accountability
kp.d: King & Spalding’s June 14, 2024 secondary account reports that the Fifth Circuit declined the proposal on June 12, 2024 after considering comments and AI use in legal practice. The quoted announcement rejects a special rule at that time, not existing obligations to check filings or sanctionable misconduct. The document supplies this decision through the client alert rather than a separately reproduced primary decision.
qs: The court, having considered the proposed rule, the accompanying comments, and the use of artificial intelligence in the legal practice, has decided not to adopt a special rule regarding the use of artificial intelligence in drafting briefs at this time.
Parties and counsel are responsible for ensuring that their filings with the court, including briefs, shall be carefully checked for truthfulness and accuracy as the rules already require.
‘I used AI’ will not be an excuse for an otherwise sanctionable offense.

kp.k: Opponents argued existing professional rules already suffice
kp.d: Brian King, the Institute for Justice, Norton Rose Fulbright’s commenters, Andrew Lee and others argued that accuracy and responsibility attach to filings irrespective of drafting tools. Some commenters relied on Civil Rule 11; others explicitly distinguished district-court obligations from appellate signature and disciplinary provisions. These are commenters’ legal arguments, not findings that every cited provision applies identically across courts.
qs: The existing rules, and duties of counsel are already very clear.

But this responsibility is already codified in Rule 11 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which applies to filings in the district court, and Rule 32(d) of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure, which applies to filings on appeal.
An additional, AI-specific order requiring another certification subject to the threat of sanctions would be redundant.

kp.k: Technology-neutral verification was a prominent alternative
kp.d: Judge Xavier Rodriguez, writing for himself and Professor Maura Grossman, proposed certification of citation and legal-analysis accuracy without identifying AI use. Carolyn Elefant and Thomas Wright similarly argued that inaccurate citations predate generative AI and that any new verification obligation should cover human-produced as well as AI-produced material. These alternatives separate verification of work from disclosure of tools.
qs: On behalf of myself and Prof. Maura R. Grossman of the Univ. of Waterloo, we respectfully suggest the following to be technology neutral in tone.
Additionally, counsel and unrepresented filers must further certify that all citations and legal analysis has been reviewed for accuracy.

Additionally, counsel and unrepresented filers must further certify that all text, whether generated by human or artificial intelligence, including all citations and legal analysis, has been reviewed for accuracy and approved by a human.

kp.k: Human review alone raised competence and delegation concerns
kp.d: Alan Goldstein, Lance Stevens, Martin Stern and Carlton Fields commenters challenged the adequacy of approval by an unspecified human. Suggested alternatives included an admitted attorney or supervised reviewer, the lead signing lawyer, and the unrepresented filer personally. Stevens supported the proposal with this qualification; Goldstein emphasized that counsel should remain responsible for represented parties’ submissions.
qs: I do not believe "by a human" is a strict enough standard.
If the filer is unrepresented by counsel, I would think that the filer, not “a human,” would be the person who must review the generative AI material for accuracy and approval.
Respectfully, lawyers, not just anybody, should be responsible for the content of submissions to the U.S. Court of Appeals when the filer is represented by counsel.

kp.k: Stronger skeptics distinguished verification from substantive legal judgment
kp.d: Peter Winders reported that Carlton Fields prohibited generative AI in producing legal work. Forwarded views from Gary Sasso and Steven Dupre argued that checking whether cited authorities exist and are accurately described cannot replace independent research, identifying omitted favorable or adverse authority, reconciling doctrines, and developing better arguments. Their categorical claims about AI’s inability to think are advocacy in the comments, not empirical findings.
qs: In our firm, we have adopted a policy that GenAI not be used at all in production of legal product, and we have viewed with dismay the pronouncements of some lawyers that GenAI is reformative rather than potentially destructive to quality lawyering.

What this means is, you can ask ChatGPT to write a Fifth Circuit brief, and then ask a first year associate to cite check the authorities set forth in that brief to make sure (1) they exist and (2) the brief accurately reports what they say.

The Court and its constituents deserve to be given the best possible work product by the parties’ legal counsel, not some “app” that some “human” certifies they have “reviewed for accuracy” and “approved.”

kp.k: Embedded AI complicates reliable use disclosure
kp.d: Elefant, Coale, Wright, the Institute for Justice, Norton Rose Fulbright’s commenters and Campbell argued that generative features embedded in search, research and word-processing products make use difficult to identify. They questioned whether reading generated search answers, revising wording, generating tables, rejecting suggestions or editing away generated text would trigger certification. These comments identify anticipated compliance problems, not measured compliance costs.
qs: The rule would also impose an impractical burden by expecting lawyers to somehow discern when a research tool relies on generative AI, which is often proprietary or opaque.
Second, it’s not clear when a lawyer “uses” generative AI.
In this environment, even the most conscientious attorney will have trouble knowing for sure what software may use a “generative” feature, and how the software may do so if it does.

kp.k: Team drafting creates AI provenance tracking burdens
kp.d: The Institute for Justice described a prospective workflow in which AI-generated research language enters an internal memorandum and subsequently a brief drafted by another lawyer who does not know its origin. It argued that tracking this provenance could require cumbersome internal disclosure systems even when the final authorities and arguments have been checked. This is a hypothetical organizational mechanism, not evidence that particular firms implemented such systems.
qs: As a result, that second attorney may submit a brief containing AI-generated text without knowing it.

Short of law firms imposing cumbersome internal disclosure requirements for tracking the use of AI-generated text in internal memos, it is hard to see how those lawyers could comply with the proposed rule.
And assuming they have confirmed the accuracy of the citations and legal arguments, it is hard to see why this Court would care that this accurate text was composed, in part, by a computer.

kp.d: The Institute for Justice distinguished outsourcing research, reasoning and drafting from using AI to clarify an already-written passage. It predicted that undifferentiated disclosure could discourage the latter by making responsible users fear judicial skepticism. Its fallback recommendation was a conditional accuracy affirmation that would not affirmatively disclose whether AI was used. Norton Rose Fulbright’s commenters and Lee similarly predicted chilling effects on adoption.
qs: IJ’s primary concern with the proposed rule is that it treats all uses of generative AI as equivalent and equivalently worthy of disclosure.
Suggest ways to make this section clearer and more concise, without changing its meaning.
This narrower affirmation addresses the Court’s concerns without outing the filer as having used generative AI.
Some attorneys might believe that checking the box in Form 6 that generative Al was used will be perceived negatively by some judges and law clerks.

kp.k: Certification could generate collateral disputes and privilege concerns
kp.d: Coale and Wright predicted tactical disputes over AI use, drafting history and compliance rather than filing quality. Coale cited a dispute over double-spacing as an analogy and criticized AI-detection reliability. Wright characterized disclosure as an invasion of work product; Elefant was more qualified, acknowledging that research tools probably are not protected while warning that disclosure could expand toward prompts and research strategy. These are predicted risks and legal positions, not adjudicated privilege holdings.
qs: I’m concerned that the proposed rule is redundant of rules and risks unwanted satellite litigation.
Compounding the difficulty in defining that line, recent experience shows that software claiming to “detect” the use of generative AI is notoriously inaccurate.
A lawyers’ chosen research tools probably do not qualify as work-product privilege.
If courts can require disclosure of use of AI tools, will compelled disclosure of prompts and search strategy – activities which indisputably fall within work product privilege – soon follow?

kp.k: Hallucination incidents supported competing regulatory interpretations
kp.d: Peter Wechsler supported certification and submitted materials describing fabricated citations and Judge Brantley Starr’s district-court requirements. An attached Reed Smith account of Mata v. Avianca reports a $5,000 joint-and-several penalty and emphasizes both failed verification and subsequent misleading conduct. Opponents interpreted such incidents as reasons to enforce existing duties; Lee argued that anecdotes alone should not drive circuit-wide rulemaking. These incidents are not measurements of model hallucination rates.
qs: I am in favor of your court amending it's rules to require an AI certification.
A penalty of $5,000 was imposed jointly and severally on the law firm and individual attorneys.

First, attorneys have a responsibility to verify all court submissions. Second, if an error is discovered, be honest, and immediately work toward correcting it to avoid more severe damages to all concerned.
Only data—and not anecdotes—should drive a rule change that affects such an important court as the Fifth Circuit.

kp.k: Starr’s requirements illustrate a distinct district-court approach
kp.d: The attached judge-specific requirements require an appearance-stage certificate covering future filings and verification through print reporters or traditional legal databases. They name ChatGPT, Harvey.AI and Google Bard as generative tools and warn about hallucinations and bias. This is a separate district judge’s regime, not an adopted Fifth Circuit rule, and its requirements should not be conflated with the circuit’s abandoned proposal.
qs: All attorneys and pro se litigants appearing before the Court must, together with their notice of appearance, file on the docket a certificate attesting either that no portion of any filing will be drafted by generative artificial intelligence (such as ChatGPT, Harvey.AI, or Google Bard) or that any language drafted by generative artificial intelligence will be checked for accuracy, using print reporters or traditional legal databases, by a human being.
These platforms in their current states are prone to hallucinations and bias.
On hallucinations, they make stuff up—even quotes and citations.

kp.k: AI assistance extends beyond inserting generated prose
kp.d: Lee described proposed or available uses including reviewing appellate records, summarizing transcripts, comparing briefs, testing reply arguments, locating contract clauses, translation and legal research. He argued that the rule could require certification even when generated text never enters the filing. These capability claims and workflow recommendations support augmentation of lawyers’ work, not autonomous responsibility for filed briefs.
qs: Other generative AI uses include assisting review of a voluminous appellate record to locate key provisions or to summarize lengthy trial transcripts.

Even a single dense contract could benefit from GAI analysis—to locate the choice of law provision, for instance, to compare it against an earlier version, or to summarize complex legal language in “lay English.”
Powerful generative AI tools offer many capabilities that result in “generated text”—but the practitioner may not necessarily use that “generated text” in the filed document.

kp.k: Guidance and supervision were proposed instead of certification
kp.d: Campbell recommended definitions, best practices and guidance as alternatives to mandatory disclosure. Lee emphasized technology competence, candor and supervision, distinguishing the ABA’s model-rule amendment from state adoption and reporting that forty states, including Louisiana and Texas, had adopted the technology-competence amendment. He endorsed Judge Arun Subramanian’s approach of permitting tools while requiring counsel personally to confirm research accuracy.
qs: Given the above, rather than the Proposed Rule, the court could instead provide a list of guidelines for using generative AI.
Forty states including Louisiana and Texas have adopted the 2012 amendment, known as the “duty of technology competence.”
Use of ChatGPT or other such tools is not prohibited, but counsel must at all times personally confirm for themselves the accuracy of any research conducted by these means.
Using two different platforms is advantageous but does not replace the need for reflective thinking about the research problem and answers.

kp.k: Attached interview qualifies claims about autonomous legal drafting
kp.d: The July/August 2023 Colorado Lawyer attachment presents Harry Surden’s assessments, Ronald Sandgrund’s questions and commentary, and separately labeled ChatGPT-3.5 responses. Surden describes GPT-4 as more useful than GPT-3.5, while cautioning against directly using general-purpose tools with private client information and recommending legal-technology services with additional safeguards. The attachment’s questions about malpractice, lawyer displacement and access to justice, and its AI-generated answers, are exploratory material rather than empirical findings or the Fifth Circuit’s views.
qs: I would not recommend that lawyers use ChatGPT-3.5 or GPT-4 directly today.
If they enter in private or sensitive client information to OpenAI, they could run afoul of ethical privacy rules, and may even effect a waiver of confidentiality privileges.
I think the technology needs some good, independent testing before we can advocate using it more broadly.
I expect these types of programs to only get better, in terms of usefulness and accuracy, overtime.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The compilation presents competing claims about AI-assisted legal work, the consequences of mandatory disclosure, and the continuing responsibility of human filers.
pts.d: The Fifth Circuit's November 2023 proposal would have required counsel and unrepresented filers to certify either non-use of generative AI in drafting or human verification and approval of generated text. It was not a ban. The June 2024 decision, reproduced in King & Spalding's secondary account, declined a special rule while maintaining responsibility for accurate filings. Carlton Fields' Gary Sasso, whose comments Peter Winders endorsed, argues that checking citations alone leaves essential research, identification of alternative and adverse authorities, and strategic analysis undone; Winders reports a firm prohibition on using generative AI to produce legal work. Goldstein, Stevens, Stern and Dupré question whether review by any human is an adequate professional safeguard. Conversely, Rodriguez and Grossman propose technology-neutral verification. King, Cottle, Coale, Wright, Elefant, the Institute for Justice, Norton Rose Fulbright, Campbell and Lee argue in different ways that existing professional duties already cover inaccurate AI-assisted work. Elefant, Shanks, Coale, Wright, IJ, Norton Rose Fulbright, Campbell and Lee predict that ambiguous disclosure requirements could create compliance burdens, discourage beneficial adoption, or provoke collateral disputes. Elefant and Wright also raise work-product concerns. IJ distinguishes outsourcing research and reasoning from using AI to improve already-written prose, arguing that a uniform disclosure requirement may stigmatize the latter. Lee claims AI can assist research, record review, translation, summarization and argument development. In the attached Colorado Lawyer interview, Professor Harry Surden describes GPT-4 as useful for first drafts, subject to human checking and additional analysis, and anticipates improving usefulness and accuracy. He identifies potential to make law more accessible and understandable, but calls for independent comparative testing. Ronald Sandgrund's conclusion predicts near-term augmentation rather than wholesale replacement, while leaving the timing and shape of larger changes uncertain. The interview's ChatGPT-3.5 responses separately speculate about cheaper document production and improved access to justice, alongside unequal access to tools, increased low-quality filings, and possible shifts in legal employment; these are model-generated statements, not Surden's findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The record principally offers rule texts, professional judgments, examples, judicial incidents and cited authorities; it does not provide controlled evidence that AI certification improves filings or that predicted burdens would occur.
pts.d: The proposed rule and Form 6 directly establish the contemplated certification requirement. The declination is supplied through a June 14, 2024 client alert quoting the court, rather than a separately reproduced primary decision. Its reference to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 6(b)(1)(B) should be preserved as the supplied account's wording, not treated as independently verified authority for general filing accuracy. Commenters' references to Civil Rule 11 should likewise remain attributed; IJ, Norton Rose Fulbright and Lee distinguish district-court rules from appellate provisions. Wechsler supports certification through attached materials describing fabricated-citation incidents and Judge Brantley Starr's district-court requirements. The Reed Smith attachment reports a $5,000 joint-and-several sanction in Mata v. Avianca and emphasizes both fabricated authorities and subsequent misleading conduct. Elefant cites cases involving inaccurate authorities predating ChatGPT and describes her own uncertainty about research-tool functionality. Coale uses a dispute about double-spacing as an analogy for potential satellite litigation. IJ supplies hypothetical drafting and team-workflow scenarios, supported by product announcements. Lee cites vendor developments, law-firm adoption reports and a Bloomberg Law survey conducted in September–October 2023: as he reports it, respondents used AI for legal research (53%), summarizing legal narratives (42%), reviewing documents (34%) and due diligence (21%); 25% of in-house respondents reported company purchase or investment in a generative-AI tool. The excerpt does not supply sufficient sampling or denominator detail to generalize those figures to all lawyers. Sasso's claims rest on professional judgment and a conceptual account of model limitations, not comparative testing. Surden invokes his research and technical expertise but supplies no test protocol or measured brief-quality results in the interview, expressly calling for independent testing. Sandgrund's broader forecasts are synthesis and speculation. ChatGPT-3.5's interview answers are generated conjectures, not independent empirical evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The core policy debate concerns late 2023 and early 2024; the attached capability discussion concerns 2023-era models, and most forecasts lack fixed deadlines.
pts.d: The proposal was issued in November 2023, with comments due January 4, 2024. The June 12, 2024 declination was explicitly qualified as a decision not to adopt a special rule 'at this time', not a permanent prohibition on future regulation or an endorsement of unchecked AI output. Predictions about administrative burden, chilling effects and satellite litigation were conditional on adoption of the proposed language and increasing integration of generative AI into everyday software. IJ anticipates that some lawyers will use such features unknowingly, including through colleagues' research memos. Lee's adoption figures refer to September–October 2023, not current usage. The attached July/August 2023 Colorado Lawyer article distinguishes the free GPT-3.5 from GPT-4 released in March 2023. Surden's first-draft assessment depends on case complexity, substantial human checking and analysis, and privacy-protective legal technology rather than direct entry of sensitive client material into consumer tools. His expected improvements have no specified deadline. Sandgrund's augmentation forecast is near-term and qualified; the longer-term employment scenarios posed to ChatGPT-3.5 are conditional on AI assuming more lawyer-like functions. Judge Starr's attached assessment concerns platforms 'in their current states' and his own district-court practice, not an adopted Fifth Circuit rule.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are appellate filers, lawyers working in teams, clients and courts; the attachments additionally discuss underserved people and legal workers.
pts.d: The proposed certification expressly covered counsel and unrepresented filers, with possible striking of documents and sanctions for material misrepresentation. Goldstein would allocate review to an admitted attorney or directly supervised person when a client is represented, and to the filer when unrepresented; Dupré would place it with the lead signing lawyer. Sasso warns that clients and courts could receive inadequately reasoned briefs even when a junior associate checks existing citations. IJ highlights supervising and drafting lawyers who may unknowingly incorporate AI-generated material from colleagues, and lawyers using AI solely for clearer prose. Elefant, Wright and Coale anticipate burdens affecting drafting strategy, disclosure disputes and litigation costs; Shanks and Norton Rose Fulbright predict consequences for client service and useful technology adoption. Courts and opposing parties may have to handle fabricated authorities or additional compliance disputes. Lee's survey discussion separately concerns law-firm practitioners and in-house counsel on the corporate buyer side. Surden's access-to-justice discussion concerns people unable to obtain or afford legal help, not merely corporate cost reduction. Sandgrund anticipates augmentation for practicing lawyers while noting possible exposure of legal assistants. The model-generated interview discussion speculates about disadvantaged litigants, wealthier parties able to buy better tools, prospective lawyers and legal education. These possibilities are not demonstrated employment or access-to-justice outcomes.
